explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF sends row-count messages for statements in the procedure, adding unnecessary client traffic.
With XACT_ABORT OFF, some run-time errors abort only the failing statement and leave its transaction open.
@CustomerIdText fixes the later customer lookup to customer 1 rather than using the procedure input.
@OrderID starts with the unexplained business key 1, which can remain in use if subsequent queries return no rows.
SELECT * returns every Sales.Orders column, including large text fields, and makes the result depend on the table schema.
TOP (10) has no ORDER BY, so the selected order IDs can vary between executions.
DISTINCT is redundant because Sales.Orders.OrderID is the primary key and no join can duplicate it.
NOLOCK can return uncommitted Sales.Orders rows or miss or duplicate rows during concurrent writes.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) applies a function to the filtered column instead of expressing the condition as a date range.
The filter fixes the reporting year at 2016 rather than taking it as input.
SQL Server implicitly converts the nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText to int to compare it with Sales.Orders.CustomerID.
The OR-based customer filter combines a scan case with an equality lookup, which can lead to a plan that performs poorly for one case.
LIKE N'%urgent%' searches anywhere in Comments and cannot use an ordinary index prefix seek.
ISNULL unnecessarily wraps the non-nullable, indexed CustomerID column instead of comparing it directly.
The predicate filters for the embedded customer ID 1 rather than using @CustomerID.
Adding zero to OrderID does not change its value and obscures a direct primary-key comparison.
CustomerID <> 1 can match most of Sales.Orders, making the predicate poorly selective.
The query excludes customer ID 1 without identifying why that customer is special.
The CROSS JOIN pairs orders with unrelated customers; TOP limits the output but does not establish a relationship.
TOP (1) has no ORDER BY, so the chosen order and customer pair is arbitrary.
The comma join separates the Orders-OrderLines relationship from the table list, making the join condition easier to overlook.
TOP (1) does not specify which matching order to return.
The scalar OrderLines count depends on each outer OrderID and can require repeated lookups instead of one grouped aggregation.
The EXISTS check depends on each outer OrderID. Joining to distinct qualifying OrderIDs would preserve one result per order.
The qualification rule embeds an unexplained Quantity threshold of 1.
The CASE expression that produces HasComments is repeated in ORDER BY, so the two expressions can drift apart.
ORDER BY 2 sorts on OrderDate only as long as it remains the second selected column.
OrderDate is not unique, so orders with the same date can move across page boundaries without a tie-breaker such as OrderID.
Each branch selects a different primary-key value, so UNION performs unnecessary duplicate elimination.
The first UNION branch fixes the lookup to order ID 1.
The second UNION branch fixes the lookup to order ID 2.
COUNT(*) > 0 counts matching order lines when the query only needs to know whether one exists.
The unfiltered SELECT can assign many OrderIDs to @OrderID. The retained value depends on row processing order and is later used by writes.
The insert into @OrderIds takes five orders without specifying which five.
SELECT INTO infers the schema of #ImplicitOrders from the query rather than declaring it explicitly.
The query populates #ImplicitOrders with five orders chosen without a defined order.
The cursor selects two orders without ORDER BY, making the OrderID returned by its single fetch arbitrary.
The statement concatenates the converted @CustomerID into SQL text, producing a different statement for each value.
EXEC runs the customer lookup as a string without binding CustomerID as a parameter.
The statement embeds the converted @OrderID in the SQL text rather than keeping the statement text constant.
sp_executesql is called without parameter definitions or bound values for the order lookup.
#Scratch is explicitly created but not explicitly dropped, so it remains allocated until procedure scope ends.
The handler returns the error message as a result row without rethrowing or signaling failure to the caller.
The negative-order-ID check uses RAISERROR rather than THROW; RAISERROR does not honor XACT_ABORT.
PRINT sends a buffered text message rather than a structured diagnostic.
The query fixes the lookup to customer ID 1 instead of using the available @CustomerID parameter.
The Orders query embeds an unexplained cutoff of January 1, 2016.
Without a conversion style, '01/02/2016' can mean January 2 or February 1 depending on the session date format.
TOP (1) has no ORDER BY to determine which order from the invoice join is returned.
COALESCE wraps Sales.Orders.CustomerID in the join even though the column is non-nullable, obscuring a direct comparison on the indexed key.
COALESCE wraps Sales.Invoices.CustomerID in the join even though the column is non-nullable, obscuring a direct comparison on the indexed key.
Joining Sales.Orders to itself on its primary key adds no information because only the original OrderID is selected.
TOP (1) has no ORDER BY, so the self-join does not select a predictable order.
Sorting all orders by the nvarchar(max) Comments column can require substantial memory and spill to tempdb.
SUM(Quantity) processes the entire Sales.OrderLines table because there is no filter.
HAVING filters on the grouping key OrderID, not on an aggregate, so the condition can be expressed in WHERE before grouping.
The query assumes only positive OrderIDs should be included, but the table definition does not require positive keys.
The unfiltered COUNT(*) has to count all rows in Sales.Orders.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns one row, so ordering by OrderCount cannot affect the result.
MERGE adds complexity and exposes this update-only operation on Sales.Orders to MERGE-specific edge cases.
The matched MERGE action assigns Comments to itself and can still incur write overhead or fire update triggers.
SET Comments = Comments leaves the value unchanged but can still acquire locks, generate log records, and fire triggers.
Deleting by Quantity rather than an order-line key can remove matching lines across unrelated orders.
The delete treats Quantity = -1 as a deletion marker without documenting that business rule.
WAITFOR DELAY keeps the request waiting for one second and ties up a SQL Server worker.
The transaction starts outside TRY/CATCH, so there is no local exception handler to ensure rollback if execution fails before it reaches ROLLBACK.
The procedure enables IDENTITY_INSERT on Sales.Orders even though it performs no identity insert before turning it off.
sp_who is called without its sys schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is not reset within the procedure, so it can silently cap subsequent queries and writes at one row.
The VALUES insert into #DemoCategories depends on the table's column order to map the category ID and name.
The insert assigns the unexplained fixed CategoryID 99 regardless of @NewCategory.
Prepending '%' to @CustomerName prevents a prefix seek on the Sales.Customers.CustomerName index.
Caller-supplied @CustomerName is concatenated into a quoted SQL literal before execution, allowing input to change the SQL statement. Bind the LIKE pattern as a parameter instead.
sp_executesql is invoked without its sys schema qualifier.
The update has no predicate to target a customer. With ROWCOUNT 1 still active, it can change an arbitrary row in #DemoCustomers.
The update assigns the unexplained fixed CustomerCategoryID 1.
The WHERE predicate on o.OrderDate drops customers with no matching order, effectively turning the LEFT JOIN into an inner join.
The customer-orders query embeds an unexplained cutoff of January 1, 2016.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN and does not match rows; IS NULL is the correct null test.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) can run once per customer row unless SQL Server can inline the scalar function.
If the delete or commit fails, the CATCH block does not check transaction state or roll back, so it can leave an open transaction.
The handler returns ERROR_MESSAGE() as a result row but does not tell the caller that the transactional delete failed.
WITH (INDEX = 1) forces clustered-index access and prevents the optimizer from choosing the CustomerName index.
Three derived-table layers repeat the same CustomerID projection and can be replaced with a single query.
LIKE '%A%' searches anywhere in CustomerName and cannot use an ordinary prefix seek.
SELECT * makes the result depend on every column exposed by dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti.

The name dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti suggests a multi-statement TVF, but its definition is not supplied. If it is multi-statement and can be expressed as one query, an inline TVF would give the optimizer more visibility.
